visual.general_description: Open operative field with red/yellow tissue held over an abdominal incision.
visual.detailed_description: A single color operative photograph shows a central open incision in brown skin surrounded by blue drapes. Multiple pale surgical gloves surround the incision. A gloved hand at upper right holds an elongated red/yellow lobulated tissue segment above the opening; another hand near upper left holds a ring-handled instrument. Two broad metal retractors pull the skin/incision margins apart. A white handled tool with a blue tip approaches the lower tissue from image left, with a blue cord behind the hands. Small red spots and wet reflective tissue are visible. There is no panel letter, scale, caliper, arrow or printed numerical defect measurement. The source identifies incarcerated omentum; appearance alone is not used to diagnose ischemia or bowel viability.

visual.detailed_description: A single pink-purple photomicrograph shows a dense oblique band of cellular/fibrous tissue extending from upper right to lower left, with many dark oval nuclei and pink wavy matrix. Several pale rounded/oval spaces occur along the left and lower-left margins. A large round/oval red-filled lumen near lower center has a pale gap in its red contents; smaller red-filled spaces occur nearby. A ragged tissue edge borders white background at the right. There is no pixel-printed magnification, scale bar, arrow or panel letter. H&E and ×100 are caption claims; no malignancy, necrosis or infection diagnosis is independently made from this one field.

evidence.quote: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained photomicrograph of the hernia sac wall with associated fibroadipose tissue (×100 magnification).Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained photomicrograph demonstrating the histologic architecture of the hernia sac wall. The image shows dense fibrocollagenous tissue with interspersed adipose lobules. Areas of vascular congestion, focal hemorrhage, and dilated blood vessels are present, findings consistent with ischemic changes secondary to incarceration. No evidence of malignancy, necrotizing infection, or alternative pathologic processes is identified.
